title: Spaced revision timetable
examples: Should I study all my maths topics on one day?
What is the difference between spaced and massed practice?
How do I make a revision plan that actually works?

explain.say: Today we are learning about smart revision techniques. These methods help you remember things better. We will look at spacing, interleaving, and planning backwards.

items: Planning Backwards: Working from the end date

explain.say: Spacing means reviewing material over increasing time gaps. Instead of cramming, you spread out your study sessions. For example, if you learn about fractions today, you should review them a few days later.
Interleaving means mixing different types of problems in one session. You do not study one topic until you are finished with it. For example, mix questions on fractions with questions on decimals.
Planning backwards means starting with your exam date. You then work back to decide what you need to study each week. For example, if the exam is in four weeks, you plan your first study session now.
In real life, imagine you are learning to drive a car. You should not only practice parallel parking on one day. You should mix it with starting on hills and changing gears.
A common mistake is only reviewing the things you already know well. This gives you a false sense of security. Instead, try to mix topics and review older material regularly.

items: Don't just look at what is easy
Mix hard and easy topics together
Always look back at old notes

faq.q: Should I use all three techniques for every subject?
faq.a: You do not need to use all three every single day. It is best to use spacing for general review, interleaving for practice sessions, and planning backwards to structure your whole timetable.
asks: Which technique is best for maths?
Do I need to do all three methods?

faq.q: If I have a big exam next month, where should I start planning?
faq.a: You should always start by looking at the exam date. This helps you break down the whole amount of work into manageable chunks over time.
asks: How far back should I plan?
What is the first step for a big exam?

faq.q: What is the difference between spaced and massed practice?
faq.a: Massed practice means studying one thing for a very long time in one sitting. Spaced practice means studying that same thing in shorter sessions spread out over many days.
asks: What is the opposite of cramming?

faq.q: When I mix topics, should I mix them randomly?
faq.a: It is better to mix topics that are related or at a similar difficulty level. This helps your brain switch gears between ideas smoothly.
asks: Can I mix science and history?
How random should the mixing be?

faq.q: Does planning backwards mean I can skip topics?
faq.a: No, planning backwards helps you see what you cannot skip. It forces you to allocate time for every necessary topic before the exam date.
asks: Is planning backwards a strict schedule?

facts: Spacing helps move information into long-term memory.
Interleaving improves your ability to choose the right method.
Planning backwards ensures all topics are covered before the test.
Reviewing material over time is more effective than cramming.

quiz.say: If you learn about verbs on Monday, and then review them on Wednesday and Saturday, what technique are you using?
quiz.why: This method spreads out your review sessions over time, which is the definition of spacing.

wrong.0: Planning backwards is about setting the overall schedule from the exam date, not the review action itself.
wrong.1: Massed practice means studying everything at once, which is the opposite of what you are doing.
wrong.3: Interleaving means mixing different types of topics, not just reviewing one topic over time.

quiz.say: You are revising for a test covering algebra, geometry, and statistics. You spend one hour doing a mix of problems from all three areas. What technique is this?
quiz.show: Mixing related topics in one session
quiz.why: Mixing different subject areas or topic types within one study session is called interleaving.

wrong.0: This describes the action of studying, not the structure of the study session itself.
wrong.1: Cramming is studying everything intensely in one block of time, which is not the goal here.
wrong.3: Spacing requires you to wait several days between reviewing the same topic, not mixing it right now.

quiz.say: Your final exam is scheduled for the end of the month. What should your very first revision step be?
quiz.show: Start with the final exam date

options.show: Start by reviewing the easiest topic
options.say: Start by reviewing the easiest topic

options.show: Just study the hardest topic first
options.say: Just study the hardest topic first

quiz.why: Starting with the final date allows you to work backward to set realistic goals for every week leading up to it.

wrong.1: This approach ignores the overall timeline and might lead to forgetting harder topics later.
wrong.2: While important, this ignores the need to build a schedule that covers all required material.
wrong.3: This is massed practice and does not account for the necessary time gaps for memory consolidation.
